interviewQuestions.question: How would you prevent two users from booking the same seat at the same time?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by naming the actual bug: a check-then-act read of seat status followed by a separate write leaves a race window where two requests can both pass the check. So the fix is to fold the check into the write itself — an atomic conditional update like `UPDATE seats SET state='HELD' WHERE seat_id=? AND state='AVAILABLE'` — and look at rows-affected instead of doing a prior read.

I'd walk through why an in-process lock (`synchronized` on a `Show` object) isn't enough once there's more than one app server — each server's lock only protects its own process, so the race just moves to the database, which is where the real fix has to live.

I'd close by covering holds: every hold needs a server-enforced TTL, checked lazily on next access, so abandoned checkouts don't lock out inventory forever.

**Testing:** whether you can name the exact race condition and push the fix down to an atomic database operation, rather than answering "use a lock" without specifics.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Preventing concurrent double-booking

interviewQuestions.question: How would you handle a flash sale for a blockbuster's opening show?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this as: the general design already works for 99% of shows — the flash sale only breaks it because a handful of the best seats suddenly see extreme contention from thousands of requests in seconds. So I'd scope the fix to that specific hotspot rather than redesigning the whole system.

Concretely: a virtual waiting room or rate limiter in front of checkout smooths the request burst; shortening the hold TTL during the sale window frees contested seats faster; and for the specific hot seats, I'd consider a lightweight in-memory queue per seat instead of raw database contention, since retrying a database write thousands of times per second on the same row wastes capacity.

I'd also flag that this is a temporary, predictable spike — over-engineering the steady-state design for it is the wrong trade.

**Testing:** whether you can scale the one hot path precisely instead of proposing a blanket, always-on solution.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Scaling for a blockbuster opening
